strengths: Identifies a concrete and interesting phenomenon (feature magnitude divergence to million-scale and channel-wise entropy collapse) in IR Transformers using LayerNorm, and provides a plausible causal analysis linking it to per-token normalization and input-blind rescaling, consistent with related findings in GANs/diffusion models.

The proposed i-LN is simple, easy to implement as a drop-in replacement, and is well motivated by two clearly articulated design principles (spatially holistic normalization and input-adaptive rescaling).

Extensive empirical validation across multiple IR tasks (SR, denoising, deraining, JPEG artifact removal), multiple backbones (SwinIR, HAT, DRCT), and multiple normalization baselines (RMSNorm, LayerScale, ReZero, InstanceNorm, BatchNorm, no-norm) under a controlled, reimplemented training protocol for fair comparison.

Interesting auxiliary analyses: bias-alignment/compensatory mechanism visualization (Fig.7), RPE structure analysis (Fig.9), and especially the low-precision inference experiments showing i-LN prevents FP16 overflow artifacts and quantization degradation — a practically relevant contribution beyond just PSNR gains.
Ablation on the rescaling component (LN* vs i-LN) isolates the contribution of each proposed modification.
Clear and well-organized writing supported by good visualizations of training dynamics.
weaknesses: Performance gains over vanilla LayerNorm, while consistent, are often fairly small in several tasks (denoising, JPEG artifact removal), raising the question of whether the improvement is primarily attributable to training stabilization/better optimization rather than a fundamentally superior inductive bias; this is not clearly disentangled from other confounds like effective learning rate changes due to different normalization statistics.

The explanation for why per-token normalization causes divergence and why holistic normalization fixes it is largely qualitative/hypothesis-based (i.e., 'networks attempt to bypass constraints'); a more rigorous theoretical or causal analysis (e.g., gradient-level or optimization-landscape argument) is missing, weakening the scientific rigor of the central claim.

Comparisons to only InstanceNorm and BatchNorm as 'spatially consistent' alternatives are somewhat narrow; other batch-free instance-level normalization variants (e.g., GroupNorm variants, PixelNorm) are not considered, which could better isolate the contribution of the holistic-normalization idea versus the rescaling idea.

Reliance on relatively small-scale training settings (300K iterations, specific patch sizes) that differ from typical SOTA training recipes (no progressive patch size, no mixed augmentation) could limit generalizability of the absolute PSNR gains to fully-tuned SOTA pipelines, and results are only shown on two/three backbones, limiting broader claims about generality across all IR Transformer architectures.
The claim about 'improved spatial correlation modeling' via RPE structure is based on qualitative visual inspection only (Fig.9), without a quantitative metric to substantiate the claim.

No computational/memory overhead analysis of i-LN (e.g., additional cost of computing/storing a rescaling term per attention/FFN layer) relative to vanilla LayerNorm is reported, despite motivating efficient inference use cases.

Some claims (e.g., 'first to reveal' or novelty framing) could be viewed as incremental relative to prior works (EDM2, DRCT, EDSR) already noting feature-magnitude issues and normalization-related artifacts in related domains; the paper's contribution is more of a careful empirical synthesis/adaptation to IR Transformers rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: Identifies and clearly documents an interesting empirical phenomenon (extreme feature magnitude divergence and channel-wise entropy collapse) in IR Transformers trained with conventional LayerNorm, supported by extensive visualizations across layers, iterations, network scales, and four different IR tasks.
The proposed i-LN is simple, requires no additional parameters beyond the existing LayerNorm affine terms, and is presented as a drop-in replacement, making it easy to adopt in practice.

Broad experimental coverage: three backbones (SwinIR, HAT, DRCT), four IR tasks (SR, denoising, deraining, JPEG artifact removal), and comparison against many alternative normalization/stabilization schemes (RMSNorm, LayerScale, ReZero, InstanceNorm, BatchNorm, no-norm).

Interesting and practically relevant finding that i-LN substantially improves robustness under reduced-precision (int8/int4/fp16) inference, which is a meaningful applied contribution for edge deployment.
Reasonably thorough ablations (rescaling on/off, entropy analysis, RPE structure, network-scale robustness) that attempt to dissect which component of i-LN drives the gains.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: i-LN is essentially a combination of already-known ideas (instance/holistic normalization similar to InstanceNorm/BatchNorm variants already tested in Table 1, plus a rescaling strategy conceptually similar to LayerScale/AdaIN-style input-adaptive scaling). The paper does not clearly justify why this particular combination is superior to IN/BN plus rescaling, beyond empirical results.

The causal narrative ("networks bypass LayerNorm by amplifying specific channels") is supported only by correlational evidence (bias-channel alignment in Fig.7) rather than a controlled causal experiment; the anthropomorphized framing throughout the paper (network "attempting" or "sneaking" values) is not rigorously substantiated.

Since i-LN computes normalization statistics over the entire spatio-channel dimension, it removes per-token normalization entirely. All experiments are trained and largely evaluated with statistics computed over fixed, small training patches (64x64 or 128x128); it is unclear how normalization statistics computed globally over an image generalize to inference on full-resolution test images of highly variable size and content, which is a significant open concern for a method claiming to be a general drop-in replacement.

Performance gains are inconsistent in magnitude across tasks; for denoising and JPEG artifact removal, improvements are often within ~0.05-0.1 dB, and no statistical significance testing (multiple seeds, confidence intervals) is provided, making it hard to assess whether these differences are meaningful versus noise.

Related work coverage on normalization specifically tailored to Transformer-based image restoration architectures (e.g., Restormer's own normalization design choices, other recent variants) is thin, making it hard to judge how i-LN compares against already-existing IR-specific normalization schemes rather than just generic normalization baselines.
No analysis of computational/memory overhead or throughput of i-LN relative to vanilla LayerNorm, despite the paper emphasizing deployment/efficiency considerations (low-precision inference).
Perceptual quality metrics (e.g., LPIPS) are absent; only PSNR/SSIM are reported despite qualitative figures suggesting visually perceptible differences that PSNR/SSIM may not fully capture.

strengths: Thorough and systematic empirical investigation of feature divergence in IR Transformers, verified across varying network depth, width, backbones (SwinIR, HAT, DRCT), and four distinct IR tasks (SR, denoising, deraining, JPEG artifact removal).

The proposed i-LN is simple, easy to implement as a drop-in replacement, and is compared against a wide array of alternative normalization/stabilization schemes (RMSNorm, LayerScale, ReZero, InstanceNorm, BatchNorm, no-norm), giving good context for its relative benefits.

Interesting supporting analyses beyond raw metrics: the bias-alignment analysis (Fig. 7) offering a plausible mechanistic explanation for how LayerNorm bypass occurs, and the RPE structure visualization (Fig. 9) as indirect evidence for improved spatial correlation modeling.
Practically relevant finding regarding robustness under low-precision (int4/int8/fp16) inference, which has clear deployment value for IR models on edge devices.
Reasonable ablation isolating the two proposed components (holistic normalization vs. input-adaptive rescaling), showing each contributes to the overall gain.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: normalizing across spatio-channel dimensions closely resembles Instance/Group-style normalization, and the rescaling term resembles AdaIN/LayerScale-like schemes; the novelty largely lies in combining and analyzing these ideas for IR Transformers rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Performance gains are uneven across tasks — substantial for SR and deraining but quite marginal for denoising and JPEG artifact removal (often <0.1 dB), which is somewhat inconsistent with the abstract's claim of 'substantial performance gains' across all IR tasks.
No variance/error bars or multiple training seeds are reported, making it hard to assess whether the smaller reported gains (e.g., CAR, DN) are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run noise.

The causal claim that networks 'intentionally bypass' LayerNorm is supported only by correlational evidence (bias-magnitude alignment); no ablation or intervention experiment directly tests this causal hypothesis (e.g., synthetically constraining channel entropy).

Missing comparison/discussion against Restormer's channel-only LayerNorm variant, which was specifically designed to address related spatial-context issues in IR Transformers and is a natural relevant baseline.
Limited discussion of computational/memory overhead or any efficiency trade-offs introduced by the holistic normalization and rescaling operations relative to vanilla LayerNorm.

strengths: Identifies and carefully documents an interesting empirical phenomenon in IR Transformers trained with vanilla LayerNorm: feature magnitude divergence to million-scale accompanied by channel-wise entropy collapse, supported by visualizations across network depth, width, and task types.

Provides a reasonably rigorous theoretical treatment (Propositions 1 and 2 with full proofs in the appendix) showing that per-token LayerNorm fails to preserve inter-pixel/spatial structure up to a homothety, while the proposed spatially holistic variant does.
The proposed i-LN is simple, is a drop-in replacement for vanilla LayerNorm, and is motivated by a clear two-part design (spatial holisticness + input-adaptive rescaling), each ablated separately.

Extensive empirical validation: multiple backbones (SwinIR, HAT, DRCT, SRFormer), multiple IR tasks (SR, denoising, deraining, JPEG artifact removal), multiple scales (lightweight to full-sized HAT), low-precision/quantized inference, real-world degradation (Real-ESRGAN pipeline), and multi-seed/multi-batch-size stability analysis.

Careful comparison against a wide range of alternative normalization and stabilization schemes (RMSNorm, InstanceNorm, BatchNorm, ReZero, LayerScale, gradient clipping, KL regularization), which strengthens the case that the proposed combination is a meaningful design choice rather than an arbitrary one.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter and training configuration tables for every model variant used across the paper.
weaknesses: Reported quantitative gains are often quite small in absolute PSNR/SSIM terms (e.g., ~0.02–0.3 dB in several SR/DN/CAR settings, including the full-sized HAT results in Table 6), raising questions about the practical significance of the fix relative to the dramatic ('million-scale') framing of the underlying problem.

The core method is a fairly straightforward combination of known ideas (global/holistic normalization akin to instance/group norm, plus a rescaling term reminiscent of adaptive/conditional normalization), so the technical novelty is somewhat incremental despite the thorough empirical package.

No comparison against more modern or higher-capacity IR architectures mentioned in related work (e.g., Restormer, Uformer) — all experiments use Swin-style hybrid attention backbones (SwinIR/HAT/DRCT/SRFormer family), limiting evidence of generality across architecture families.

Most main-text tables report single-run point estimates without variance/error bars; multi-seed variance analysis is only provided for one specific setting (HAT1, ×4 SR, Urban100) in the appendix, and even there the real-world SR experiment (Table 9) shows substantial run-to-run variance that is not statistically contextualized.

No discussion of computational/memory overhead of i-LN (e.g., additional cost of computing global mean/std over the full spatio-channel dimension and the extra rescaling multiplication) relative to vanilla LayerNorm, which would be relevant for practitioners.

The paper does not benchmark against other spatially holistic normalization variants beyond InstanceNorm/BatchNorm (e.g., GroupNorm), which would help isolate exactly which design choices in i-LN are responsible for the gains.

Some claims (e.g., 'robustness under RealWorld IR tasks' and improved spatial correlation modeling via RPE visualization) are largely qualitative/illustrative rather than rigorously quantified, which somewhat weakens the strength of the broader claims made in the abstract and conclusion.

strengths: Identifies and carefully documents an interesting phenomenon: feature-magnitude divergence and channel-entropy collapse under vanilla per-token LayerNorm in IR Transformers, supported by visualizations across network depth/width/task/backbone (Fig. 1, 2).

Provides a simple, drop-in normalization scheme (i-LN) with a clean theoretical motivation via two propositions showing per-token LN fails to preserve inter-pixel structure while holistic normalization preserves it up to scale.

Very extensive empirical program: multiple backbones (SwinIR, HAT, DRCT, SRFormer), multiple tasks (SR, denoising, deraining, JPEG artifact removal), ablations isolating the two proposed components (spatial holisticity and rescaling), comparisons against many alternative normalization schemes (RMSNorm, InstanceNorm, BatchNorm, LayerScale, ReZero, no-norm) and alternative stabilization techniques (gradient clipping, KL regularization).

Additional robustness studies are appreciated: low-precision/quantized inference, multiple random seeds, varying batch size, and real-world (Real-ESRGAN) degradation pipeline, which go beyond typical ablation depth in this subarea.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables for every model variant and training configuration are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: In the most realistic, extensive-computation setting that matches official public model training budgets/warm-start (Table 6), the improvements from i-LN shrink to near-negligible levels (e.g., x2 SR Set5 38.63→38.65, x4 Urban100 27.97→28.04), which undercuts the practical significance of the method once models are trained under standard, well-tuned regimes rather than the lightweight/reduced-budget configurations used for most of the paper's headline results.
Gains are inconsistent and modest for several tasks (denoising, JPEG artifact removal), by the authors' own admission, weakening the claim of broad applicability across IR tasks.

The theoretical contribution (Propositions 1–2) is elementary — essentially showing per-token normalization is not an isometry/homothety while a global-statistic normalization trivially is — and does not provide deep insight into why or when this mismatch actually harms restoration quality, nor a formal explanation of why feature magnitudes diverge in the way observed.

Much of the causal narrative ("networks attempt to bypass LN's constraints", bias-alignment as a "compensatory mechanism") is interpretive/hypothesis-driven rather than rigorously validated; the paper largely relies on visual/qualitative correlations (RPE structure, entropy plots) rather than controlled causal experiments.

The proposed method is conceptually close to existing spatially-holistic normalization schemes (InstanceNorm/BatchNorm), which the paper's own Table 1 shows already outperform vanilla LN; the incremental novelty over combining known holistic normalization with a simple adaptive rescale is limited.

No comparison against other recent, more sophisticated Transformer training-stabilization techniques beyond RMSNorm/ReZero/LayerScale/GC/KLD (e.g., QK-norm, sandwich norm, other structured init schemes used in large-scale ViT training) that could also address the same magnitude-divergence issue.

Quantitative tables generally lack variance/error bars except in a couple of dedicated robustness sections, making it hard to assess whether the often small PSNR/SSIM gains are statistically meaningful.

strengths: Identifies and clearly diagnoses a previously underexplored phenomenon (extreme feature magnitude divergence and channel-wise entropy collapse) in LayerNorm-based Image Restoration Transformers, with compelling visualizations (Fig.1-2) across network depth/width/task/normalization variants.

Provides a reasonably principled theoretical framework (inter-pixel structure preservation via homothety) to explain why per-token LN disrupts spatial correlations, with formal propositions and proofs for both vanilla LN and the proposed LN*.
Proposes a simple, easily-adoptable drop-in replacement (i-LN) combining spatially holistic normalization with input-adaptive rescaling, which is intuitive and lightweight to implement.

Very extensive empirical validation: multiple backbones (HAT, SwinIR, DRCT, SRFormer), four IR tasks (SR, denoising, deraining, JPEG artifact removal), multiple normalization baselines (RMSNorm, InstanceNorm, BatchNorm, RZ, LayerScale, no-norm), alternative regularizers (gradient clipping, KLD), low-precision/quantized inference, multi-seed and multi-batch-size robustness studies, and real-world degradation (Real-ESRGAN pipeline) experiments.
Good ablation study isolating the contribution of spatial holisticity vs. rescaling, supported by both quantitative (entropy/PSNR) and qualitative (RPE structure, SR crops) evidence.

Reasonable reproducibility: detailed appendix with full hyperparameter/training configurations for each model variant and scale of experiments (Type1/2/3 settings), plus scaling experiments matching official full-sized HAT training budgets.
weaknesses: Quantitative PSNR/SSIM improvements from i-LN are often modest (sometimes well under 0.5 dB, particularly for denoising and JPEG artifact removal), and the significance of such gains is not rigorously supported with confidence intervals/statistical tests in most tables (only Fig.11 explores seed variance, and only for one setting).

The theoretical contribution (Propositions 1-2) is a fairly direct algebraic consequence of per-token vs. global mean/variance computation and does not by itself explain why LN drives magnitudes to a literal million-scale; the causal link between structure-preservation failure and the observed extreme divergence remains largely hypothesized/correlational rather than proven, despite the interesting compensatory bias-alignment analysis (Sec 4.4.2).

Baselines are all self-reimplemented under a common (often lightweight, non-warm-started) training recipe; there is limited comparison to actual published SOTA numbers or verification that the reported gains persist under the exact state-of-the-art training pipelines (progressive patch sizing, mixing augmentation, warm-start), aside from one HAT† scaling experiment.

No discussion of computational/memory overhead of computing statistics over the full spatio-channel dimension (versus per-token LN), which could matter for large feature maps in practical deployment—this practical cost-benefit tradeoff is unaddressed.

The related work / positioning section is relatively brief and does not deeply engage with other normalization-free or alternative-normalization IR architectures (e.g., dense residual designs, other AdaLN-style conditioning schemes used in generative/diffusion restoration) beyond a short paragraph.

i-LN closely resembles known ideas (InstanceNorm/BatchNorm-style holistic statistics combined with AdaLN/scale-modulation-like rescaling), so novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior normalization literature, even though its application and diagnosis within IR Transformers is new.
